abstract: Apolipoprotein A-I (apoA-I) is the main protein of high-density lipoprotein and is comprised of a helical bundle domain and a C-terminal (CT) domain encompassing the last ~65 amino acid residues of the 243-residue protein. The CT domain contains three putative helices (helix 8, 9, and 10) and is critical for initiating lipid binding and harbors sites that mediate self-association of the lipid-free protein. Three lysine residues reside in helix-8 (K195, 206, 208), and three in helix-10 (K226, 238, 239). To determine the role of each CT lysine residue in apoA-I self-association, single, double and triple lysine to glutamine mutants were engineered via site-directed mutagenesis. Circular dichroism and chemical denaturation analysis revealed all mutants retained their structural integrity. Chemical crosslinking and size-exclusion chromatography showed a small effect on self-association when helix-8 lysine residues were changed into glutamine. In contrast, mutation of the three helix-10 lysine residues resulted in a predominantly monomeric protein and K226 was identified as a critical residue. When helix-10 glutamate residues 223, 234, or 235 were substituted with glutamine, reduced self-association was observed similar to that of the helix-10 lysine variants, suggesting ionic interactions between these residues. Thus, helix-10 is a critical part of apoA-I mediating self-association, and disruption of ionic interactions changes apoA-I from an oligomeric state into a monomer. Since the helix-10 triple mutant solubilized phospholipid vesicles at higher rates compared to wild-type apoA-I, this indicates monomeric apoA-I is more potent in lipid binding, presumably because helix-10 is fully accessible to interact with lipids.

Site-directed mutagenesis, recombinant protein expression and purification
The coding sequence for His
6
-tagged human apoA-I was inserted into a pET-20b(+) expression vector (Eurofin Genomics, Ebersberg, Germany). Using Quikchange-II site-directed mutagenesis (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA), lysine or glutamate to glutamine substitutions were introduced into the CT domain. Mutations were verified by DNA sequencing (Genewiz, La Jolla, CA). ApoA-I was expressed in
Escherichia coli

This culture was used to inoculate 500 mL broth cultures and which were grown in a benchtop shaker at 37 °C. Protein overexpression was induced with 0.5 mM isopropyl-β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (Gold Biotechnology, St. Louis, MO) when the optical density of
E. coli
cultures at 600 nm reached 0.6. The cells were collected by centrifugation at 8000
g

g
at 4 °C to remove cellular debris. The supernatant was mixed with an equal volume of sample loading buffer (2× PBS, 6 M guanidine-HCl) and loaded onto a 5 mL HiTrap chelating column (GE Healthcare, Piscataway, NJ). , 1 mM EDTA, pH 7.8, lyophilized, and stored at −20 °C. Protein fractions were assessed for purity by sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE). Verification of the desired mutations was determined by MALDI-TOF analysis of enzyme digests. Proteins were digested with trypsin (trypsin gold mass spectrometry grade, Promega, Madison, WI) or endoproteinase Glu-C (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO) for 24 h at 37 °C in 50 mM NH

After Ziptip cleanup (Millipore Corporation, Billerica, MA), the samples in 0.1 % trifluoroacetic acid (Fisher Scientific, Fair Lawn, NJ) were directly spotted on MALDI target plates, mixed with α-cyano-4-hydroxy cinnamic acid matrix (Protea Co, Morgantown, WV) in 50 % acetonitrile (Millipore Corporation, Billerica, MA) and 0.1 % trifluoroacetic acid (Fisher Scientific, Fair Lawn, NJ) and then analyzed on an AB 4800 MALDI TOF/TOF mass analyzer (Applied Biosystems, South San Francisco, CA) at the CEPA Proteomics core facility at CSU Long Beach. Mass spectra were collected from 1000 laser shots per spot and tandem mass spectrometric (MS/MS) data were collected from 2000 laser shots in the 4800 mass analyzer.

2.3.
Gel electrophoresis
SDS-PAGE analysis was used to determine protein purity and to assess the degrees of self-association in crosslinking experiments. To separate proteins on SDS-PAGE, 15 μg of protein was incubated at 70 °C for 10 min with lithium dodecyl sulfate sample loading buffer and NuPAGE sample reducing agent (Life Technologies, Grand Island, NY). Proteins were separated on a 10 % Bis-Tris gel (NuPAGE) in MES buffer at 200 V for 30 min, and visualized by incubation with 5 % naphthol blue-black (m/v) in 45 % methanol, 45 % Milli Q water, and 10 % acetic acid.
2.4.
Self-association analysis
To analyze the degree of self-association, each protein sample was subjected to crosslinking with dimethylsuberimidate (DMS) (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA). Proteins (15 μg in 30 μL, 0.5 mg/mL) were incubated in the presence of 13 mM DMS for 1.5 h at 24 °C in 63 mM triethanolamine, pH 9.0, and analyzed by SDS-PAGE as described above. SEC was also used to determine protein self-association. Each protein sample was diluted in PBS to a concentration of 0.5 mg/mL and 550 μL was loaded onto a Superdex 200 increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare, Pittsburgh, PA) using a fast protein liquid chromatography (FPLC) system (Bio Rad, Hercules, CA). Samples were eluted for 60 min at a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min while the absorbance was monitored at 280 nm.
2.5.
Phospholipid solubilization
To measure the interaction of apoA-I with phospholipids, large unilamellar vesicles (LUV) were prepared through extrusion. Ten mg of 1, 2-dimyristoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DMPC) (Avanti Polar Lipids, Birmingham, AL) was dissolved in 500 μL of a 3:1 mixture of chloroform to methanol, which was subsequently dried with a stream of N
2
, forming a thin lipid film, which was further dried for 3 h in a lyophilizer. Dried lipid films were resuspended in 1 mL PBS, incubated for 1 min in a 37 °C water bath and subsequently vortexed for 1 min. The suspension was then passed 17 times (at 45 °C) through a 200 nm polycarbonate membrane pore, using the Avanti Polar Lipids mini extruder. In a 500 μL quartz cuvette (Starna cells, Atascadero, CA), 25 μL LUVs (250 μg DMPC) was equilibrated with 350 μL of PBS at 24.1 °C until the absorbance at 325 nm remained constant for 5 min. Protein in PBS (125 μL of a 2 mg/mL solution) was transferred into the cuvette, mixed with the LUVs, and the change in absorbance was measured at 325 nm using a Genesys 150 UV–Visible spectrophotometer equipped with a Peltier cell holder unit (ThermoFisher Scientific). First order rate constants (k) were calculated based on the decrease in absorbance.

1.
Introduction
ApoA-I is the primary protein component of high-density lipoproteins (HDL) and plays a critical role in reverse cholesterol transport, in which cholesterol from peripheral tissues is transported to the liver for processing and excretion as bile [
1
]. ApoA-I has been studied extensively for its role in cholesterol transport processes, including promoting cholesterol efflux, serving as a critical cofactor for cholesterol esterification, and facilitating lipid cargo into the hepatocyte intracellular space [
2
–
5
]. Human apoA-I is a 243 residue, 28 kDa apolipoprotein comprised of amphipathic α-helical segments and exists in lipid-free, lipid-poor, and lipid-rich forms [
6
]. Upon acquiring phospholipids the protein forms discoidal HDL, and upon incorporation of cholesterol and cholesterol esters HDL becomes spherical. Lipid free apoA-I is composed of two distinct domains. The N-terminal (NT) domain (residues 1–178) provides structure and stability to the protein and harbors lecitin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) activity, while the small CT domain (residues 179–243) is responsible for initiation of lipid binding, facilitating transition from a lipid-free to a lipid-poor form. The CT domain also harbors sites for self-association, facilitating formation of oligomers at a protein concentration above 0.1 mg/mL [
6
–
12
]. While X-ray structures of an N-terminal deletion variant (Δ1–43) and the CT-domain deletion variant (Δ185–243) have been obtained, acquisition of the lipid-free full-length structure of apoA-I has proved much more challenging due to the dynamic conformation of apoA-I and its propensity to form oligomers [
5
,
13
]. Recently, a consensus model of lipid free apoA-I has been proposed, based on cumulative structural studies published over the past 40 years [
1
,
14
–
16
]. This consensus model suggests an ordered NT helical bundle with a CT domain devoid of secondary structure.
When the six lysine residues that reside in the CT domain of apoA-I were substituted by glutamine, this resulted in significantly reduced levels of self-association and the appearance of a predominantly monomeric protein. This could be due to elimination of the positive charge of the ε-amino groups, disrupting salt bridge formation which may play a role in apoA-I self-association. To gain insight into the role of positively charged residues of the CT domain in self-association, it is necessary to identify the critical lysine residues [
17
]. A site-directed mutagenesis strategy was employed to assess the role of each of the six lysine residues of the CT domain in single-lysine mutants, while double and triple lysine mutants were designed to assess the collective contribution of two clusters of lysine residues. This provided evidence that lysine residues at the far CT end of the protein are critical for apoA-I self-association.

3.
Results
3.1.
Mutation design
Early analysis of the apoA-I amino acid sequence revealed a pattern of 11 or 22 amino acid repeats separated by proline side-chains. The protein includes ten of these repeats, which are predicted to be class A amphipathic α-helices. These ten helices are preceded by one class G α-helix. Three of the putative α-helices are located in the CT domain: a 22-residue helix-8 (H8, residues187–208), an 11-residue helix-9 (H9, residues 209–219) and a 22-residue helix-10 (H10, residues 220–241) [
18
]. The CT domain of apoA-I harbors a total of six lysine residues, three in H8 at position 195, 206, 208; and three in H10 at position 226, 238 and 239 (
Fig. 1
). The apoA-I variant with all six CT lysine residues changed to glutamine (6KQ-apoA-I) was predominantly monomeric [
17
]. However, the contribution of each individual residue for self-association was not known. Therefore, six single variants were generated, each with a lysine to glutamine mutation (KQ). To examine the role of the H8 and H10 lysine residues, two triple mutants were engineered, each containing three KQ mutations in either H8 (3KQH8-apoA-I, with K195Q, K206Q, and K208Q mutations) or H10 (3KQH10-apoA-I, with K226Q, K238Q, and K239Q mutations). ApoA-I lacking CT mutations (WT-apoA-I) and 6KQ-apoA-I were used as controls, representing the self-associated and monomeric form of the protein, respectively. The apoA-I variants were expressed in
E. coli
and purified by nickel affinity chromatography and SEC, and protein purity was confirmed by SDS-PAGE. The mutations were then verified by MALDI-TOF analysis of trypsin and or Glu-C digests of the variants, in addition to DNA sequencing.
3.2.
Structural analysis
While the CT domain is poorly structured, it was still necessary to verify that the mutations did not disrupt the overall protein fold. To this end, Far-UV CD was employed to determine the secondary structure of the two triple mutant proteins in comparison to WT-apoA-I and 6KQ-apoA-I. The ellipticity of the proteins was measured from 185 to 260 nm; Far-UV CD spectra showed characteristic troughs at 208 and 222 nm for WT-apoA-I, illustrative of a highly α-helical protein (
Fig. 2
). Both triple mutants displayed spectra similar compared to WT-apoA-I and 6KQ-apoA-I. Total α-helical content was calculated using the molar ellipticity value at 222 nm (
Table 1
). The apoA-I samples exhibited helical content values ranging from 49.4 to 52.0 %, similar to the results obtained by the previous KQ mutations [
17
]. This confirmed that multiple KQ mutations in the CT domain of apoA-I did not significantly alter the secondary structure of the protein. Since triple and sextuple KQ mutations did not cause significant changes in secondary structure, Far-UV CD spectra of the single lysine mutants were not collected.
To further examine the mutants for potential changes in protein stability, proteins were chemically denatured, and their unfolding was followed by CD spectroscopy. The proteins were incubated with increasing concentrations of guanidine-HCl, and their ellipticity was measured at 222 nm to determine loss of α-helical structure. All proteins displayed a denaturation profile similar to that of WT-apoA-I (
Fig. 3
). The midpoint of denaturation of each protein was calculated using sigmoidal curve fitting (
Table 1
). This [Gdn-HCl]
½
concentration represents a 50 % loss in helical structure and was used as a measure of protein stability. The [Gdn-HCl]
½
values of WT and mutant apoA-I were 1.0 M, suggesting no change in protein stability caused by the multiple mutations in the CT domain.
The % α-helix was calculated using the molar ellipticity at 222 nm, the error represents standard deviation with
n
= 3. The midpoint of guanidine-HCl denaturation was the average of two trials and determined by sigmoidal curve fitting. Rate constants of DMPC solubilization were determined assuming first order reactions (±standard deviation with
n
= 3).
3.3.
Lipid binding analysis
In addition to the site of oligomerization, the CT domain of apoA-I is also known to initiate lipid binding, a critical step in formation of discoidal HDL [
3
,
8
,
9
,
12
,
19
]. To determine if the mutations affected lipid binding, the interaction with phospholipid bilayer vesicles was analyzed. Phospholipid binding interaction was measured by monitoring the vesicle disappearance when apoA-I transformed DMPC LUVs into discoidal HDL particles. This transition was monitored by the absorbance at 325 nm over the course of 200 s. Protein was added to a suspension of DMPC LUVs in PBS (1:1 final mass ratio of protein to lipid with a final protein concentration of 0.5 mg/mL) at the DMPC gel-liquid crystalline phase transition temperature (24 °C). Addition of WT-apoA-I or apoA-I mutants to DMPC vesicles resulted in a rapid decrease in sample turbidity, and the phospholipid vesicle suspension became optically clear within 100 s (
Fig. 4
). This showed that the mutants were able to transform LUVs into discoidal HDL efficiently, indicating the KQ mutations in the CT domain did not cause disruption of lipid-protein interactions. When rate constants of LUV solubilization for each protein were determined, this showed that WT and 3KQH8-apoA-I displayed slower rates compared to 6KQ-apoA-I and 3KQH10-apoA-I (
Table 1
).
3.4.
Self-association analysis
To determine the effect of the mutations on the oligomerization of apoA-I, single and triple KQ mutants were subjected to DMS crosslinking of apoA-I and subsequently analyzed by SDS-PAGE. Crosslinking of WT-apoA-I showed the 28 kDa apoA-I band, plus four additional protein bands, representing dimers, trimers, tetramers, and presumably pentamers (
Fig. 5
). Thus WT-apoA-I exhibited a high degree of intermolecular crosslinking, which was expected since the protein concentration used was larger than 0.1 mg/mL at which concentration it is known to self-associate [
13
]. DMS-treated 6KQ-apoA-I displayed very little intermolecular crosslinking, consistent with earlier results demonstrating the protein is predominantly monomeric. The crosslinking pattern displayed by the single KQ mutants treated with DMS was similar compared to WT-apoA-I, however, the multimeric protein band intensity slightly decreased with a corresponding increase in the intensity of the 28 kDa band. This slightly lower crosslinking efficiency indicated that each mutation had a small effect on apoA-I self-association. The 3KQH8-apoA-I mutant displayed a similar crosslinking pattern compared to WT-apoA-I with minor changes in crosslinking efficiency as observed for the single KQ mutants. In contrast, the 3KQH10-apoA-I mutant displayed a significantly reduced level of intermolecular crosslinking, similar as observed for 6KQ-apoA-I. Thus, the oligomeric state of 3KQH10-apoA-I shifted towards a monomeric state which suggests the three H10 lysine residues are critical in facilitating protein self-association. Since DMS targets lysine residues to crosslink proteins, which were removed in the mutagenesis approach, additional self-association studies were necessary.
To further characterize the self-association properties of the mutant proteins, protein samples were analyzed via SEC. The elution profile of WT-apoA-I displayed a broad band with the main peak eluting at 12.0 mL (
Fig. 5
&
Table 2
), indicative the protein is present as multiple oligomeric states, in agreement with the DMS crosslinking analysis. The 6KQ-apoA-I mutant displayed a distinct peak at 14.7 mL, which was identified previously as a monomer by MALS [
17
]. The elution profiles of H8 single mutants K195-, K206-, and K208Q-apoA-I resembled that of WT-apoA-I indicating these mutants remained largely oligomeric. In agreement with the DMS crosslinking analysis, small increases in elution volumes were observed and the single KQ mutants eluted between 12.2 and 12.8 mL. However, the H10 single mutants K226-, K238-, and K239Q-apoA-I experienced much larger retention volumes of 14.2, 13.5, and 13.3 mL, respectively. K226Q-apoA-I displayed the largest increase in elution volume of the single mutants; this indicated a critical role of K226 for self-association although substitution alone was not sufficient to generate a monomeric state. 3KQH8-apoA-I showed a moderate increase in elution volume (13.7 mL), indicating that while three H8 substitutions had a more pronounced effect, the protein remained in an oligomeric state. In contrast, 3KQH10-apoA-I showed a marked increase in elution volume to 14.8 mL. The sharp elution peak of 3KQH10-apoA-I presented a near identical overlap with 6KQ-apoA-I suggesting this triple mutant is predominantly monomeric. Thus, the self-association studies show that the H10 lysine residues play a collective and critical role in the self-association of apoA-I. While the triple mutant with H10 residues K226Q, K238Q, and K239Q shifted the equilibrium towards a monomeric state, substitution of K226 alone could not accomplish this. To evaluate if two KQ mutations were sufficient, three additional double mutants were generated via site-directed mutagenesis: K226,238Q-,K226,239Q-, and K238,239Q-apoA-I. DMS crosslinking showed monomer, dimer, trimer, tetramer, and pentamer bands for these double mutants, but compared to WT-apoA-I, they displayed strong reduced intensities of the inermolcular crosslinked bands (
Fig. 6
).
In comparison, trimer, tetramer, and pentamer bands were absent in 3KQH10-apoA-I and 6KQ-apoA-I. This suggests that while two lysine substutions substantially reduced apoA-I self-association compared to K226Q-apoA-I, it was insufficient to generate a monomeric form of apoA-I. SEC analysis showed that double mutants K226,238Q-apoA-I and K226,239Q-apoA-I exhibited near identical peak profiles, indicating a similar extent of self-association (
Fig. 6
). The elution volume peaked 0.2 mL before 6KQ-apoA-I, resulting in an incomplete overlap (
Fig. 6
,
Table 2
). This indicates that while the double KQ mutants were predominantly monomeric, some self-association did still occur. Since K238,239Q-apoA-I eluted before the other double mutants, this confirmed that K226 is the most critical lysine residue for apoA-I self-association.
3.5.
Ionic binding partner analysis
The decrease in self-association observed for the KQ mutants may be due to disruption of ionic bonds between oppositely charged residues. The primary sequence of H10 shows three glutamate residues (E223, E234, & E235) in close proximity to the three H10 lysine residues, and thus have potential to form a salt bridge with each other. To address this, three single glutamate mutants were generated: E223Q-, E234Q, and E235Q-apoA-I. Self-association properties were determined by DMS crosslinking and SEC. To allow for direct comparison, the single KQ mutants of H10 were included in the analysis. The EQ single mutants displayed DMS crosslinking patterns similar to the lysine single mutants (
Fig. 7
), showing a slight increase in the monomeric population compared to WT-apoA-I. SEC analysis showed E223Q-apoA-I eluted at 13.8 mL (
Table 2
), and the elution profile was similar to that of K226Q-apoA-I, indicating both mutants possess similar degrees of self-association. The elution profile of E234Q-apoA-I was similar to that of K238Q-, and K239Q-apoA-I, with an elution volume of 13.5 mL. E235Q-apoA-I had the smallest elution volume at 13.0 mL, suggesting a relatively small contribution to self-association. Thus the results of the EQ single mutants showed that E223 behaved very similar compared to K226, indicating both residues participate in a critical salt-bridge, either with each other or with another oppositely charged residue.

Discussion
The CT domain of apoA-I is a dynamic region of the protein. It is structurally flexible and harbors sites for initiation of lipid binding and self-association [
20
]. Early characterization of apoA-I complexes by ultracentrifugation showed evidence for the presence of monomers, dimers, tetramers and octamers [
21
]. Previously, we demonstrated that when all six lysine residues of the apoA-I CT domain were changed to glutamine, the protein became predominantly monomeric [
17
]. The present study aimed to identify the precise lysine residue(s) that are critical for apoA-I self-association by employing a site-directed mutagenesis approach producing single, double, and triple KQ variants of apoA-I. The new variants displayed helical contents of ~50 % and [Gdn-HCl]
½
values of ~1.0 M, similar to those reported earlier for WT and previously engineered CT-apoA-I KQ variants [
17
,
22
–
26
]. Thus, the mutations in the CT domain did not disrupt the overall protein fold, and therefore did not adversely affect the NT core domain, which is mainly responsible for the stability and integrity of apoA-I [
27
]. Since the CT domain is relatively unstructured in the lipid-free state, this explains the absence of a measurable structural effect as a result of the amino acid changes [
7
,
12
,
28
].
Self-association was assessed by DMS crosslinking and SEC analysis. The results of these analyses aligned well even though DMS crosslinking efficiency depends on the abundance of exposed lysine side chains, which were reduced in number because of the KQ mutations. SDS-PAGE analysis of the crosslinked single KQ mutants showed that small increases in the intensity of the monomer protein band were accompanied with corresponding decreases in the intensity of intermolecular cross-linked protein bands. The greatest decrease in crosslinking efficiency among the single KQ mutations was observed for mutations in H10, evidenced by a larger amount of monomeric apoA-I in this variant. SEC analysis confirmed this observation and identified K226 as a key residue. Double mutants that included the K226Q mutation showed strong shifts towards the monomeric state. The K238/239Q double mutant, however, was much less effective in disrupting self-association, further emphasizing the critical role of K226 in apoA-I self-association. Electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy (EPR) studies indicated that K226 is part of an intra-molecular cluster, interacting with L163 and G217, and substitution may have disrupted this cluster and potentially affected self-association [
8
]. Alternatively, ionic interactions may have been disrupted as outlined below. Mutation of all three H10 lysine residues (K226, K238 and K239) to glutamine shifted the protein into a predominantly monomeric state. While the H8 triple KQ mutant (K196, K206, and K208) also displayed a measurable decrease in self-association, the effect was not as profound as observed for the H10 triple mutant.
To identify potential binding partners for electrostatic interactions with lysine, selected H10 glutamate residues were targeted for site-directed mutagenesis. SEC analysis showed that the E223Q mutation caused a similar increase in retention volume as observed for the K226Q mutation. These two residues reside on the same face of an amphipathic α-helix one helical turn away from each other and are thus in a favorable position for salt-bridge formation. Another potential salt-bridge may be formed between the closely spaced E234 and K238 residues, with the elution profiles of the corresponding mutant proteins nearly overlapping. These two potential salt-bridges may have a stabilizing effect on the α-helical character of H10, which forms a continuous hydrophobic surface large enough for intermolecular helix-helix interactions. Since mutations in H8 had some effect on self-association, albeit less pronounced, H8 residues may also contribute to CT-mediated self-association of apoA-I by adopting an α-helical conformation, further increasing the hydrophobic surface thereby promoting the oligomeric state.
EPR studies have shown that the CT domain can be separated into distinct structural regions [
8
]. Residues 188 to 205 lack tertiary contacts and have no ordered backbone, implying a random coil structure, while residues 208 to 219 form a β-strand. Residues 221 to 236 reside in an α-helical region, which corresponds to H10 residues 220–241 based on secondary structure predictions. Helix 10 is the most hydrophobic segment of apoA-I [
29
,
30
], and deletion of residues 231 to 243 resulted in a significant loss of lipid binding activity, suggesting this part is critical for lipid binding [
31
]. Thus, the CT domain may serve as a large flexible linker connecting the NT domain with H10, which is an α-helical lipid-binding motif that acts as a hydrophobic sensor. Upon docking onto a suitable lipid surface mediated by H10, the CT domain increases its helical content, bringing the NT domain helices in close contact with lipids, and the entire protein switches into a lipid bound conformation [
32
]. In the absence of lipids, the hydrophobic surface of H10 mediates apoA-I self-association when protein concentrations are sufficiently high, forming dimers, tetramers, and octamers. Both CT mediated self-association and lipid binding can act independent from the NT domain since a chimeric protein construct of CT apoA-I (residues 170–243) and lipid-inactivated apolipophorin III displayed strong self-association and lipid binding properties similar to that of apoA-I [
33
]. The H10 KQ mutations resulted in a small increase in the rate of lipid binding. This trend was also observed in the previous study, and may indicate that monomeric apoA-I is more lipid active [
17
]. Nevertheless, WT apoA-I in the oligomeric state is very active in converting DMPC vesicles into discoidal particles, indicating that the equilibrium between monomer and oligomers changes rapidly.
The related apolipoprotein E (apoE) has also a two-domain molecular organization, with a 4-helix bundle NT domain, and a CT domain comprised of three short helical segments [
23
,
24
]. Similar to apoA-I, the CT domain of apoE is responsible for self-association and is the site necessary to initiate lipid binding. Self-association is initiated by the most C-terminal α-helix, forming a tetrameric complex [
34
]. Prior to binding to lipids or lipoprotein surfaces, the apoE tetramer dissociates into a monomer to become lipid active [
35
]. ApoE self-association is mediated by an intermolecular helix-helix a coiled-coil mechanism, in which α-helices align in a parallel or anti-parallel orientation, held together by Van der Waals forces [
36
]. A typical CD spectrum of a α-helical protein displays minima at 208 and 222 nm; their ratio has been used as a criterion to predict coiled-coil helices, and favorable ratios were observed for apoE but not for apoA-I [
13
]. Further, amino acid sequence predictions of the apoE CT domain suggests a strong probability of coiled-coil formation [
36
]. In contrast, probability scores were much lower for various segments of the CT domain of apoA-I: 0.0 for residues 187–243 (Multicoil), 0.8 for residues 214–243 (Paircoil), and 0.5 for H8 residues 187–202 and H10 residues 224–230 (Deepcoil), indicating a much lower probability of coiled-coil formation. Thus, while the CT helices of apoA-I may not engage in coiled-coil formation, it is plausible that each apoA-I monomer donates one or more CT helices to form an intermolecular α-helix bundle to stabilize the self-associated state. In summary, we propose a model shown in
Fig. 8
. ApoA-I self-association is initiated by H10-H10 contacts driven by hydrophobic forces, while these α-helices are stabilized by inter- or intramolecular ionic bonds. The complex may be stabilized by H8 and H9 residues adopting α-helical conformation, forming a larger hydrophobic surface suitable for helix-helix interactions. The apoA-I dimers are further stabilized by forming a higher order complex of tetramers or octamers. Disruption of this CT helix bundle structure can rapidly result in dissociation into monomers, allowing the hydrophobic face of H10 to engage with suitable lipid surfaces, resulting in lipidation of apoA-I.
